implementation_notes: The JVM Kafka client is the canonical pull endpoint and its Scala API is the same loop: poll(Duration) returns a bounded batch, an empty result is the idle tick, and offsets commit after processing. Idiomatic Scala lifts that loop into a stream - Alpakka Kafka's committableSource emits CommittableMessage and commits only when the stream's commit is invoked, plainSource leaves acknowledgement to auto-commit or to the caller - and its reference.conf turns the pattern's two knobs into explicit settings (poll-interval: how often the stage calls poll; poll-timeout: how long each call may block).
code_sketch:
val consumer = new KafkaConsumer[String, String](props)
consumer.subscribe(Collections.singletonList("jobs"))
while (running) {
  val records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))   // empty batch = idle tick
  records.forEach(handle)
  if (!records.isEmpty) consumer.commitSync()           // ack after handling
}
pitfalls: poll-timeout and poll-interval are different knobs: a non-zero poll-timeout blocks the stream stage, so an oversized value stalls the whole stream rather than just the consumer.
A stage that blocks past max.poll.interval.ms stops polling while still believing it owns its partitions, so the group rebalances underneath it and commits fail.
Only one thread may use a KafkaConsumer, which in Scala means one actor or stage owns the client rather than a shared val.
